section.title: Our Eyes Look to the Lord
section.sectionRationale: The fourth of the fifteen Songs of Ascents, Psalms 120 to 134, sung by pilgrims going up to Jerusalem, placed in Book V of the Psalter, Psalms 107 to 150. Even having arrived at God's city in Psalm 122, His people still need mercy, and this short psalm turns their eyes upward in humble dependence.
section.thesis: Like a servant's eyes fixed on a master's hand, the psalmist's eyes look steadily to the LORD enthroned in heaven, pleading for mercy amid the contempt and scorn of the proud.
section.frameNote: Two movements: eyes lifted to the enthroned LORD in servant like dependence, verses 1 to 2, and the repeated plea for mercy amid endured contempt, verses 3 to 4.

units.label: I lift up my eyes to You

verses.text: I lift up my eyes to You, the One enthroned in heaven.
As the eyes of servants look to the hand of their master, as the eyes of a maidservant look to the hand of her mistress, so our eyes are on the LORD our God until He shows us {{chanan|mercy}}.

units.label: Have mercy on us, O Lord

verses.text: Have mercy on us, O LORD, have mercy, for we have endured much {{buz|contempt}}.
We have endured much scorn from the arrogant, much contempt from the proud.

chanan.gloss: To show favor, grace, or mercy. The psalmist's eyes wait on the LORD precisely for this undeserved kindness, as a servant waits on a master's hand for provision.

buz.gloss: Contempt, scorn, disdain. Doubled with a related word for scorn in verse 4, it describes the weight of mockery the psalmist and his people have endured from the arrogant.

basic.context: This short Song of Ascents shows that even God's gathered people, having just arrived in Jerusalem in Psalm 122, still live under mockery and contempt from the proud, and so still need mercy, turning their eyes to the LORD as a servant watches a master's hand.
basic.hermeneutics: It describes the real experience of enduring scorn from the arrogant, whether in exile, under foreign rule, or simply among the proud of any age, and prescribes as an abiding posture fixed, patient dependence on the LORD for mercy.
basic.originalLanguages: The psalmist pleads for chanan, undeserved favor and mercy, using the doubled buz, contempt, to underline how much scorn from the proud his people have borne, all while their eyes stay fixed on the LORD's hand like a servant's.
basic.typology: The servant's watchful eyes on the master's hand anticipate Christ, who took on the very form of a servant, and who Himself endured the scorn of the proud and arrogant at His trial and on the cross.
basic.christ: Jesus, taking the form of a servant, Philippians 2:7, endured far greater scorn from the arrogant than this psalmist, Hebrews 12:3, and yet fixed His eyes on the Father, modeling the very dependence this psalm describes.
basic.god: God is enthroned in heaven, sovereign over all, yet attentive to the watchful eyes of His servants, ready to show mercy to those who endure contempt while waiting on Him rather than retaliating.
basic.crossReferences: Philippians 2:7 shows Christ taking the form of a servant. Hebrews 12:2-3 calls believers to fix their eyes on Jesus who endured hostility from sinners. Luke 18:13-14 shows the tax collector pleading for mercy, echoing this psalm's cry.
basic.oneStory: This psalm's servant like dependence on the LORD's mercy amid scorn finds its perfect pattern and its answer in Christ, the true Servant, who endured contempt yet remained fixed on the Father and now shows mercy to all who look to Him.

context.literary:
Psalm 123 is a poem of eyes and of fullness. The word 'eyes' occurs four times in two verses: 'I lift up my eyes,' verse 1, 'the eyes of servants,' 'the eyes of a maidservant,' and 'our eyes,' verse 2. The gaze goes up, then settles on a hand, then rests on the LORD. Verses 3 and 4 answer with a different picture, a soul that is full, and what fills it is contempt. The poem is shaped like a funnel. Four verses of looking upward narrow into one cry, 'Have mercy on us, O LORD, have mercy.'

The pronouns shift as the psalm moves. Verse 1 is singular, 'I lift up my eyes,' and verse 2 turns to 'our,' so that one voice is joined by the congregation. This is a liturgical device, a leader begins and the assembly takes the prayer up as its own. The poem never states a request until verse 3, and even there the request is brief. It is a psalm that spends most of its words simply looking.

A simile does most of the work. Servants and maids look to the hand of master and mistress, and 'so' the people look to the LORD. The comparison is double, a man and a woman, a master and a mistress, which makes the picture complete and ordinary. It does not flatter the servants. They look because their well being is in another's hand. The poem then spends the second half on what happens when that dependence is not respected by others. The 'proud' and the 'arrogant' of verse 4 are the ones who feel no need to look to anyone.

The psalm has a close cousin in Psalm 120, which also ends with the lament that the singer has lived too long among people who hate peace, Psalm 120:6, and Psalm 129:1 to 2, which speaks of the same long persecution. The three psalms open their complaint with the same Hebrew word, rabbat, 'much, too much.' Psalm 123 is among the shortest in the collection, only four verses, and the poem's brevity suits its subject, a posture more than a story.
context.historical:
The psalm names no enemy, no date and no event. What it names is an experience, contempt, and a class of people, the proud. That fits the many seasons in Israel's life when a small people lived under the shadow of larger ones. Nehemiah is the clearest historical parallel. When the returned exiles began to rebuild the wall, Sanballat, Tobiah and Geshem 'mocked us and ridiculed us,' Nehemiah 2:19, and Sanballat asked whether these 'feeble Jews' could bring burnt stones back to life, Nehemiah 4:2. Nehemiah's response was a prayer very close to the psalm's, 'Hear us, O God, for we are despised,' Nehemiah 4:4. The Songs of Ascents may have been gathered in that period, and a pilgrim who had just come up to a modest city of rebuilt walls would have known that mockery well.

The heading says only 'A Song of Ascents' and names no author, unlike Psalms 122 and 124. The reader should not assume a Davidic setting, though Israel in David's day also knew plenty of contempt, such as the taunts of Goliath. The psalm's language of mockery recurs across the Psalter. 'You have made us a reproach to our neighbors, a mockery and derision to those around us,' says Psalm 44:13. 'The arrogant utterly deride me,' says Psalm 119:51, and the singer adds, 'but I do not turn from Your law.'

The imagery of the servants belongs to a real social world. Households in the ancient Near East depended on the master's provision, and a servant who wanted food, an instruction or protection looked to the master's hand. The psalm does not say which of these the servants wait for, and it does not need to. The hand might give, direct or hold back. What matters is that the servant's eyes are not on the other servants or on the neighbours, but on the one with authority. That relationship, dependence on an owner who may be gracious, is the picture Israel chose for its relationship to the LORD.
context.canonical:
Psalm 123 stands between the arrival at Jerusalem in Psalm 122 and the memory of rescue in Psalm 124. The placement is honest. Arrival does not end the struggle. The pilgrims who stood in the gates still face scorn, and the next psalm will say how close Israel came to being swallowed. The sequence teaches that the ascent is not a straight line from trouble to peace but a walk in which trust must be renewed.

The gaze of verse 1 is a motif across the Psalter. 'My eyes are always on the LORD, for He will free my feet from the mesh,' says Psalm 25:15, and 'my eyes are fixed on You, O GOD the Lord,' says Psalm 141:8. The line 'I lift up my eyes' opens Psalm 121:1 as well, where the pilgrim looks to the hills, and Psalm 123 corrects the eyes: not up to the hills but to the One enthroned in heaven. The title 'the One enthroned in heaven' belongs to the same family as Psalm 2:4 and Psalm 113:5 to 6. In Psalm 2 He laughs at the nations that conspire against Him. In Psalm 113 He humbles Himself to look at heaven and earth. Psalm 123 combines both, because the Enthroned One who laughs at the scoffers is the One who looks down on the scorned.

Israel's mercy cry sounds again in the Gospels. Two blind men cry, 'Lord, Son of David, have mercy on us!' Matthew 20:30 to 31, and ten lepers shout, 'Jesus, Master, have mercy on us!' Luke 17:13. The tax collector's prayer in Luke 18:13 is the same cry made personal: 'God, have mercy on me, a sinner!' Jehoshaphat's prayer in 2 Chronicles 20:12 says, 'We do not know what to do, but our eyes are upon You,' which is the posture of Psalm 123 in a moment of national danger. In Hebrews 12:2 the church is told to fix its eyes on Jesus, who 'endured the cross, scorning its shame.'

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author wanted the singers to learn what to do with their eyes. In a situation of mockery there are many places to look: at the mockers, to answer back or to be wounded, at oneself, to be ashamed, or at the circumstances, to despair. The psalm chooses a fourth, and it says so in a simile that no one can miss. The eyes go where the servant's eyes go, to the hand that can act.

It also wanted them to say the prayer together. The move from 'I' to 'we' in verse 2 teaches that contempt is endured in company and should be handed to God in company. A believer who lifts his eyes alone is joined by others who lift theirs. The community's identity is that of a people who wait on the LORD.

Third, the psalm teaches that mercy is the right thing to ask for. The people do not argue that they have earned relief or that their enemies deserve punishment. They ask for chanan, undeserved favour, and they say so three times. That is a statement about the covenant: God's people stand before Him as servants, not as bargainers. The poem leaves the answer unwritten, and the unwritten answer is deliberate. It trains the singers to keep looking 'until He shows us mercy,' verse 2, without telling them how long that will take. The psalm gives them words that they can sing as long as the contempt lasts.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes the suffering of a community that has been despised. It does not state that all contempt is deserved or undeserved, and it does not command the people to seek contempt. It also does not prescribe passivity in the face of injustice. Other psalms ask for rescue, and Nehemiah, who prayed in the same words, also set a guard and kept building, Nehemiah 4:9. The posture of watching is a posture of faith, not an excuse for doing nothing.

What the psalm commends is a manner of response to scorn. Believers who are mocked are invited to look to the LORD, to ask for mercy and to wait. Jesus calls His followers blessed when people insult them on His account, Matthew 5:11, and Peter notes that Christ 'did not retaliate,' 1 Peter 2:23. The passage does not teach that one must feel nothing. The word 'contempt' is repeated and the soul is described as full of it, so the psalm treats the hurt as real. Application therefore begins with honesty. A Christian who is ridiculed need not pretend it does not hurt, and may bring the hurt, in the psalm's own words, to God.

debates.question: Is this psalm's setting pre-exilic or post-exilic Israel?

views.label: Pre-exilic, reflecting hostility from neighboring peoples
views.case: Israel faced mockery from surrounding nations throughout the period of the judges and the monarchy, such as Goliath's taunts, fitting this psalm's language of scorn from the arrogant.

views.label: Post-exilic, reflecting contempt under foreign rule or from hostile neighbors like Sanballat
views.case: The specific complaint of enduring 'much contempt' fits the documented ridicule the returned exiles faced while rebuilding, as recorded in Nehemiah 4.

debates.bearing: Either setting yields the same pastoral point: God's people in every age have needed to turn contemptuous treatment into occasion for humble dependence on the LORD's mercy.

debates.question: Who are the 'proud' and 'arrogant' of verse 4: foreign oppressors or complacent insiders?

views.label: Foreign powers and hostile neighbours
views.case: The psalm sits among prayers about distance from peace and long enmity, Psalm 120:5 to 7, and the returned community faced mockery from outside as the story of Nehemiah shows, Nehemiah 2:19.

views.label: The comfortable within the community as well
views.case: The Hebrew text speaks of the scorn of those 'at ease,' the same adjective used of the complacent in Amos 6:1, who are 'at ease in Zion.' On this reading the contempt may come from Israelites who are secure and indifferent to the needs of others.

debates.bearing: The psalm does not need to decide. It teaches God's people to look up whoever is looking down on them, and it warns that the complacent are themselves the people who cannot say the psalm's prayer.

debates.question: Where does the servant's gaze go when the 'hand' is mentioned: provision, command or correction?

views.label: Provision and protection
views.case: A servant looks to the master's hand for food, safety and a share in the house, which fits the plea for mercy at the end.

views.label: Direction and discipline
views.case: A servant also watches for a signal or a rebuke, and the psalm could picture Israel in a time of discipline waiting for the master to relent.

debates.bearing: The text leaves the point open, and the open reading serves the psalm well. In every case the servant has no claim on the master except the master's own goodness, which is why the plea is for mercy.

study.originalLanguages:
The picture of verse 2 is made of two small words that carry a good deal. The first is yad, 'hand,' which in Hebrew stands for power, provision and authority as well as the body part. The eyes of the servants look 'to the hand' of their master and mistress, and the same word appears in the common idiom of Scripture for God's action, as in the 'hand' that saved Israel from Egypt, Exodus 14:30. The servants do not look at the face, which might show mood, but at the hand, which acts. The word for 'servants,' avadim, and the feminine 'maidservant,' shifchah, are ordinary terms for people who belong to a household, and the word for the mistress is a title of rank. The psalm refuses to romanticise them. These are people under authority, and the people of God are content to be like them in relation to the LORD.

The timing of the gaze is in the verb. The clause 'until He shows us mercy' is the Hebrew ad she yechonenu, with the short relative particle she and a verb from the root chanan, which is the root of chen, 'grace,' and of the Hebrew name Hannah. The eyes stay on the LORD until the moment of grace. The people do not name the date. In verse 3 the same root is doubled in the imperative, 'be gracious to us, be gracious to us,' and the repetition makes three uses of chanan within two verses. The psalm sets the same word in the mouth of the one who asks and in the verb of the one who answers.

Verses 3 and 4 use a vivid verb of fullness. The Hebrew says that the soul has been 'sated' with contempt, from the root sava, which usually refers to being satisfied with food. In Proverbs 1:31 it describes people filled with their own devices. Here the soul is not satisfied but stuffed, over full with scorn. The clause begins with rabbat, 'much, too much,' the same opening word as Psalm 120:6, 'Too long have I dwelt,' and Psalm 129:1, 'Many a time,' so the pilgrim collection has its own refrain of 'too much.' Three words for abuse appear in the closing verses, buz, 'contempt,' laag, 'scorn,' and a second use of buz, and the cumulative force is deliberate.

The last line shows two nouns for the abusers. The Hebrew speaks of the scorn of the sha'ananim, 'those at ease,' and the contempt of the proud. The word for 'at ease' is a term of complacency, the one used in Amos 6:1 of those at ease in Zion. The BSB's 'arrogant' translates the sense, but the Hebrew word also pictures people who are comfortable and who mock from a position of comfort. The Septuagint translates the plea for mercy with the verb eleeo, the same verb the blind men in the Gospels use when they cry out to Jesus, which links the psalm to the Gospel cry for mercy.

typology.type: The servant's eyes on the master's hand, Psalm 123:2
typology.fulfillment: The picture of a servant who watches the hand of his master finds its perfect form in the Servant of the LORD. Isaiah 42:1 introduces 'My Servant, whom I uphold,' and Philippians 2:7 says that Christ 'emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant.' Jesus describes His own habit of looking to the Father: 'the Son can do nothing by Himself, unless He sees the Father doing it,' John 5:19. The correspondence is exact in posture. The escalation is that the Servant never looked away, and His watching was perfect obedience rather than anxious need. The type falls short because ordinary servants watch with an eye to their own security, while Christ watched out of love, and His obedience won mercy for others.

typology.type: The soul full of contempt, Psalm 123:3 to 4
typology.fulfillment: The singer's soul is full of scorn from those at ease. Isaiah 53:3 says of the Servant, 'He was despised and rejected by men.' At His trial soldiers dressed Him in a purple robe, twisted a crown of thorns, saluted Him with 'Hail, King of the Jews!' and struck His head, Mark 15:17 to 20. Hebrews 12:2 says He endured the cross, 'scorning its shame.' The contempt of the proud in the psalm was real but partial. Christ bore a fuller measure of it, so that He could be the mercy the psalm seeks. The type is incomplete in that the psalm's people wait for relief, while Christ's contempt was the means by which relief was won.

The doubled cry 'Have mercy on us, O LORD, have mercy' is answered in the Gospels in the person of Jesus. Two blind men, sitting by the road, cry out, 'Lord, Son of David, have mercy on us!' and the crowd tells them to be quiet, but they cry all the louder, Matthew 20:30 to 31. The response is that Jesus, 'moved with compassion,' touched their eyes, and they received their sight, Matthew 20:34. The people who looked to the hand of the LORD for mercy found the hand of the Lord Jesus on their eyes. The correspondence rests on the shared cry. The escalation is that the mercy came as a person who touched them. The type falls short in that bodily mercy is only a sign of the greater mercy of forgiveness and the age to come.

typology.type: The One enthroned in heaven, Psalm 123:1
typology.fulfillment: The singer lifts his eyes to the One who sits in the heavens. In the New Testament the risen Christ has been 'seated at His right hand in the heavenly realms, far above all rule and authority,' Ephesians 1:20 to 21, and believers are told to 'strive for the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God,' Colossians 3:1. The person whom believers look to is a man who has endured contempt and now reigns. The correspondence is that the throne remains the place the eyes turn. The escalation is that the throne is now occupied by one who knows scorn from the inside, Hebrews 4:16. The type falls short in that the psalm did not know the one enthroned would be a risen human being.

study.christ:
The psalm brings us to Christ by showing a posture that He alone held without a flaw. The singers lift their eyes 'to You, the One enthroned in heaven,' and the Gospels record that Jesus did the same at the critical moments of His ministry. At the tomb of Lazarus 'Jesus lifted His eyes upward and said, Father, I thank You that You have heard Me,' John 11:41. Before the cross He 'lifted up His eyes to heaven and said, Father, the hour has come,' John 17:1. In the whole of the fourth Gospel His life is a servant's gaze on the Father's hand: 'the Son can do nothing by Himself, unless He sees the Father doing it,' John 5:19.

The psalm leads to Christ also by the contempt it names. Isaiah's Servant was 'despised and rejected by men,' Isaiah 53:3, and Philippians says that He 'emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant,' Philippians 2:7. The scorn of verses 3 and 4 is exactly the scorn the Gospels report: the soldiers who mocked Him with a purple robe and a thorn crown, Mark 15:17 to 20, the passers by and the leaders who taunted Him. What the psalm describes as a burden borne by many He bore on behalf of many. Hebrews tells readers to 'consider Him who endured such hostility from sinners, so that you will not grow weary and lose heart,' Hebrews 12:3. The psalm gives the words for that consideration, and Jesus gives it a face.

His response to contempt matches the psalm's refusal to retaliate. 'When they heaped abuse on Him, He did not retaliate; when He suffered, He made no threats, but entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly,' 1 Peter 2:23. That is the servant's gaze in the middle of a trial, eyes on the master's hand and no hand raised against the mockers.

The psalm also leads to Christ through the answer to its prayer. The people ask for mercy and wait 'until He shows us mercy.' The Gospels show who is the mercy of God in person. Those who cry 'have mercy on us' to Jesus receive it, as the blind men did, Matthew 20:34, and the tax collector who would not lift his eyes to heaven went home accepted, Luke 18:13 to 14. Hebrews adds that because He 'suffered when He was tempted, He is able to help those who are being tempted,' Hebrews 2:18, and invites us to 'approach the throne of grace with confidence, so that we may receive mercy,' Hebrews 4:16. The One enthroned in heaven is now someone who has felt scorn.

It would go too far to say that every word of the psalm is spoken by Jesus. The psalm's 'we' includes sinners who need mercy for their own sins, and Christ does not need to ask for mercy for Himself. The link is the shape of the life of faith: the servants' gaze, the burden of contempt, the cry for mercy, and the throne to which the eyes are lifted. In Christ these are all taken up, and the singers of the psalm find in Him both their example and their answer.
study.god:
The psalm opens with a title for God that sets the scale of everything. He is 'the One enthroned in heaven.' He is not reached by the roads of earth or threatened by the proud who mock His people. Psalm 2:4 uses the same expression of the LORD who laughs at those who conspire against Him, and the point is the same here. The mockers are loud, but the throne is high above them. The one who is asked for mercy does not need to be persuaded that He is stronger than the scoffers.

This high God is also a God who is looked to as a master is by servants. The simile is bold. It does not say that God needs servants. It says that those who belong to Him are in His household, that He is the one who provides and directs, and that His hand moves for them. Psalm 113:5 to 6 describes the same God, 'the One enthroned on high,' who 'humbles Himself to behold the heavens and the earth.' The throne and the stooping belong together. The same word that raises the eyes also describes the One who looks down.

He is a God of mercy. The word chanan belongs to the family of grace, and God Himself defined His name in these terms to Moses, 'compassionate and gracious,' Exodus 34:6. The psalm asks nothing other than what He has declared Himself to be. Believers who plead for mercy are not inventing a hope, they are holding God to His own self description.

He is also a God who is patient with the waiting. The psalm does not state when He will act. The servants look 'until' He does. That tells us that God does not always answer quickly, and that waiting on Him is not a sign of His absence. It is the proper form of faith in His timing.

He is concerned with how people treat the lowly. The contempt of the proud is set before Him as an offence. The Bible repeatedly says that God opposes the proud and gives grace to the humble, and the psalm assumes that the scorner is answerable to the Enthroned One. Worship that follows from the psalm is gentle and watchful: a people who bring their hurt to God, ask for mercy, and trust Him to answer in His time and way.

crossReferences.note: The previous pilgrim song lifts its eyes to the hills and asks where help comes from, then answers that it comes from the LORD. Psalm 123 begins with the same gesture and adjusts it. The eyes go straight to the One enthroned in heaven, with no detour via the hills, as if the earlier psalm had taught the lesson.

The One enthroned in heaven laughs at the nations that conspire against Him. The title appears here in a very different mood, as the one to whom the scorned look for mercy. Together the two verses show that the throne is both a threat to scoffers and a refuge to the despised.

David says, 'My eyes are always on the LORD, for He will free my feet from the mesh.' The steady gaze of Psalm 123 is not new to the Psalter. It is the standing habit of the faithful, and it is connected here to the expectation of rescue.

As the wall went up, Nehemiah prayed, 'Hear us, O God, for we are despised.' The contempt of Psalm 123:3 to 4 has a documented history, and the response Nehemiah gave was the same, bringing scorn to God and asking Him to act, while he went on with the work.

Facing a vast army, Jehoshaphat prays, 'We do not know what to do, but our eyes are upon You.' It is the servant's gaze of Psalm 123 in a crisis, where the people have no resources and every confidence rests on the one to whom their eyes are lifted.

The prophet warns 'those at ease in Zion.' The Hebrew word for those at ease is the one behind the scorn in Psalm 123:4. It warns that the comfortable can be the very people who despise others, and that complacency in the city of God is a danger for the people, not for outsiders.

Two blind men cry out for mercy and will not be silenced. Jesus touches their eyes and they receive their sight. Psalm 123 asked that the eyes lifted to the LORD would be met by His mercy, and here eyes that could not see are healed by the hand they cried to.

The tax collector would not lift his eyes to heaven and prayed, 'God, have mercy on me, a sinner!' He went home justified. The cry for mercy is the same as the psalm's, and Jesus says that mercy is given to those who bring nothing but the plea.

When Christ was abused, He did not retaliate but entrusted Himself to the One who judges justly. This is how the psalm's waiting looks in a man under attack. It also gives Christians a model for how to endure contempt without becoming contemptuous.

Christ took 'the form of a servant.' The servant imagery of verse 2 is thus taken up by the Son Himself, who did not look to a master's hand from outside the household but entered it. Believers who look to the Lord are following the one who showed what servanthood to God looks like.

The writer tells believers to fix their eyes on Jesus, who endured the cross and scorned its shame, and to consider Him who endured hostility so as not to lose heart. It is the New Testament form of the psalm's turned gaze, with Jesus as the one to look at.

study.oneStory:
The story of Scripture begins with a people who were given a place and a word, and a serpent who contested the word, Genesis 3:1. From then on the proud have mocked those who trust God. Pharaoh asked who the LORD was, Exodus 5:2, and the mockers of every age have called the faithful fools. Psalm 123 is the voice of the people at the receiving end of that contempt, and its answer is neither to match scorn nor to give up, but to look to the One who is enthroned above it.

The psalm answers what comes before it in the Psalter. Psalm 120 began with a singer far from peace, and Psalm 122 reached the city of peace. Psalm 123 says honestly that the contempt did not stop at the city gates. The people of God can be in the right place and still be despised. That prepares for the larger story of the prophets and exiles, where faithful people are mocked by those at ease, and where the remnant keeps its eyes on the LORD.

It also looks ahead to the Servant. Isaiah would write of One who was despised and rejected, who was acquainted with grief, and who bore the scorn of the world, Isaiah 53:3. In the Gospels that Servant takes the full weight of contempt, is mocked with a crown of thorns, and does not retaliate, Mark 15:17 to 20, 1 Peter 2:23. The cry 'Have mercy on us' is answered in Him, at the cross, where mercy and contempt meet.

The church lives in the same pattern while it waits. Believers are mocked, the proud are at ease, and the servants' eyes are on the Lord. Hebrews calls them to fix their eyes on Jesus, who endured and is now seated at the right hand of the throne of God, Hebrews 12:2. The end of the story is the day when the scorners are silenced and the eyes of the servants see the face of the Master. In the new creation 'He will wipe away every tear from their eyes,' Revelation 21:4, and those who looked up in a season of contempt will be the ones who see Him, Revelation 22:4.

sermon.title: Three Songs of Faith
sermon.why: Begg preaches Psalms 123 to 125 together, drawing out this psalm's picture of servant like eyes fixed on the LORD amid contempt as a pattern of faith for enduring scorn while waiting on God's mercy.

quiz.q: To what does the psalmist compare his eyes looking to the LORD?

options.text: A servant's eyes on the hand of a master, or a maidservant's on her mistress.
options.note: Verse 2 gives this exact double comparison.

options.text: A child's eyes on a distant star.
options.note: The comparison is specifically to servants watching a master's hand, not stargazing.

options.text: A soldier's eyes on the enemy line.
options.note: The image is one of humble dependence, not military watchfulness.

options.text: A farmer's eyes on the sky for rain.
options.note: That image appears in psalms about harvest, not this servant comparison.

quiz.q: What does the psalmist repeatedly ask the LORD for in verse 3?

options.text: Mercy, repeated for emphasis.
options.note: 'Have mercy on us, O LORD, have mercy' is stated twice for urgency.

options.text: Wealth and material increase.
options.note: The plea is specifically for mercy, not riches.

options.text: A new king to be appointed.
options.note: No request for a new ruler appears in this psalm.

options.text: Victory in battle.
options.note: The psalm addresses scorn and contempt, not a military campaign.

quiz.q: What has the psalmist's community endured, according to verses 3-4?

options.text: Much contempt and scorn from the arrogant and proud.
options.note: This is stated twice for emphasis across both verses.

options.text: A severe famine.
options.note: The complaint is about mockery, not hunger.

options.text: Loss of their homeland entirely.
options.note: The psalm's specific complaint is social scorn, not the loss of the land itself.

options.text: Betrayal by close family members.
options.note: The scorn comes from 'the arrogant' and 'the proud,' not specifically family.

quiz.q: Where is the LORD described as being enthroned, in verse 1?

options.text: In heaven.
options.note: The psalmist lifts his eyes to the One enthroned in heaven.

options.text: On Mount Zion alone.
options.note: Zion is significant elsewhere in the Ascents, but this verse specifically names heaven.

options.text: In the wilderness tabernacle only.
options.note: The text points to heaven, not a single earthly location.

options.text: Among the stars of the night sky.
options.note: The text says heaven broadly, not a specific astronomical image.

quiz.q: How does this psalm's servant posture connect to Christ?

options.text: Christ took the very form of a servant and endured scorn from the arrogant, yet kept His eyes fixed on the Father.
options.note: Philippians 2:7 and Hebrews 12:2-3 show this fulfillment.

options.text: It has no meaningful connection to the New Testament.
options.note: The servant imagery and endurance of contempt directly foreshadow Christ's own experience.

options.text: It shows Christ demanding honor rather than enduring scorn.
options.note: The Gospels show Christ enduring mockery humbly, not demanding honor for Himself.

options.text: It predicts the specific number of years until Christ's coming.
options.note: The connection is one of pattern and fulfillment, not a numerical prediction.

questions: The psalmist compares his dependence on God to a servant watching a master's hand. What would it look like this week to wait on God that attentively, rather than acting first on your own?

This psalm names real contempt and scorn endured from the proud. Where have you experienced that kind of mockery, and how does bringing it honestly to God, as this psalm does, change how you carry it?
The psalmist repeats his plea, 'have mercy on us, O LORD, have mercy.' Is there a need in your life right now urgent enough to warrant that kind of repeated, earnest prayer?
Christ took the very form of a servant and endured contempt far greater than this psalmist's. How does His example shape the way you respond when you are looked down on or dismissed?
This psalm moves from an individual 'I' in verse 1 to a communal 'we' and 'us' in verses 2 through 4. Who in your community needs you to lift your eyes to the LORD alongside them right now?

translationNotes.note: The double comparison, a servant to a master and a maidservant to a mistress, intensifies the picture of complete, watchful dependence rather than adding a separate example.
The repetition 'have mercy on us, O LORD, have mercy' is a Hebrew intensifying device expressing the depth and urgency of the plea, not mere redundancy.
Contempt and scorn in Hebrew describe not mild disrespect but active, disdainful mockery, the kind that wounds through ridicule rather than physical harm.
